Barter: Chapter one. Barter, and what money does.

William Stanley Jevons opened his book on money, in 1875, with a story. Mademoiselle Zélie, a singer from a Paris theatre, gave a concert in the Society Islands, in the Pacific, for a third of the takings. Her share came to three pigs, twenty-three turkeys, forty-four chickens, five thousand coconuts, and quantities of bananas, lemons and oranges. Coins were scarce on the islands, she could eat very little of it herself, and there was nobody to sell it to. So, Jevons reports, the fruit went to feed the pigs and the poultry.

Jevons named the problem: the double coincidence of wants. Suppose there are n goods, you hold one and want another, and you meet a stranger at random. Under barter, the stranger must have exactly what you want and also want exactly what you have: a chance of one over n minus one, squared. If everyone accepts one good, money, in payment, only one side has to match: you can sell to anyone who wants what you have, and buy from anyone who has what you want. With ten goods, that is one chance in 81 against one in 9. The more goods an economy has, the more it needs money.

Textbooks give money three jobs. It is a medium of exchange: people accept it in payment though they do not want it for itself, only to pass it on. It is a unit of account: with a hundred goods, prices in one unit need 99 numbers, while every pair's rate of exchange would need 4,950. And it is a store of value, if its purchasing power is stable. Bonds and houses store value; any unit can be used to count. The first job, being accepted in payment, is what makes money money.

There is a deeper way to see it. Narayana Kocherlakota proved in 1998 that money is a kind of memory. If everyone could consult a complete public record of who had given what to whom, then credit and reputation could do everything that money does: you would be served because the record shows you have served others. Money is a crude substitute for that record. Holding it shows that at some point you gave something of value in exchange for it. Yap's stones, whose owners everyone remembered, were a public ledger. So is a bank's database, and so is a blockchain.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: which good becomes money?

Your turn. The Island has three goods: salt, coconuts and fish, and three kinds of islander. Ana eats salt and can make coconuts. Bo eats coconuts and can catch fish. Dara eats fish and can make salt. Nobody eats what they make, so nobody can trade directly with the one person who wants their good and has what they want. Goods are costly to keep: salt hardly at all, coconuts a little, fish a lot, because fish spoils. Each month everyone meets one islander at random, and two swap only if both want to. Which good will islanders take, not to eat, but only to pass on? A, salt; B, coconuts; C, fish; or D, both salt and fish. Pause, and choose.

Agora runs the Island: 300 islanders of each kind, 400 months of random meetings, each swapping only when it makes them better off, given that fish spoils. Here is what gets passed on. Salt, in every such trade. Look at who holds what. Ana always holds coconuts, waiting to meet a salt-holder. Dara holds salt, which she made. And Bo holds salt half the time and fish the other half. Bo accepts salt in exchange for fish, though he cannot eat salt, because salt costs almost nothing to keep, and Dara, who wants fish, has salt. If you chose A, you were right: salt became the Island's money. Nobody decreed it. It emerged from people choosing what to accept.
KW: Chapter three. Kiyotaki and Wright: money as an equilibrium.

Now change one thing. The islanders learn to smoke fish, and it keeps far better: 0.25 a month instead of 0.6. Ana, holding coconuts, now takes fish when offered, though she cannot eat it. She speculates, because Dara, who has salt, wants fish, and will trade salt for it at once, while coconuts only buy salt from Bo's rare spare. Fish is more marketable, and now cheap enough to hold. Run the Island again: salt is passed on in 58 percent of such trades and fish in 42. The Island has two moneys. Which goods become money depends on what they cost to hold, and on what everyone else accepts.

Nobuhiro Kiyotaki and Randall Wright built this economy in 1989 to show that money can emerge as an equilibrium of search. Here is Ana's decision. Holding coconuts is worth minus their storage cost, plus what next month's meeting is expected to bring, discounted. Holding fish, the same with fish's storage cost and fish's prospects. She should take fish exactly when holding fish is worth more. With fresh fish, Agora's solution says no: by 0.63 in units of a meal. With smoked fish, given that everyone else speculates too, yes: by 0.14. Each pattern of trade is an equilibrium only if, given what everyone else accepts, nobody wants to change what they accept.

Map it. Along the bottom, what fish costs to keep; up the side, how patient the islanders are. Agora checks both patterns of trade at every point. Where fish is costly, only salt circulates. Where fish keeps well, salt and fish both do. In a thin band between them, neither pattern holds, and Ana takes fish only some of the time. The boundary moves with patience: patient islanders care more about where a good will take them, and less about this month's cost of keeping it. The Island's two cases sit on either side of the line.

Kiyotaki and Wright took one more step. Add a token that nobody eats and nobody makes, that costs nothing to keep. If everyone expects it to be accepted, it is accepted, because it buys things: fiat money is an equilibrium. But if everyone expects it to be refused, it is worthless, and that is an equilibrium too. Paper money rests on expectations, which is why chapter six's hyperinflations can destroy it. John Duffy and Jack Ochs ran this economy in the laboratory with paid volunteers. They mostly played the cheap-to-keep strategies, even in designs where speculating would have paid them more: money's emergence is easy in theory and slower in practice.
Quantity: Irving Fisher wrote the oldest equation in monetary economics in its modern form in 1911. The stock of money times velocity, how many times a year each dollar is spent, equals the price level times real output: total spending, counted two ways. As it stands it is an identity: it defines velocity. In growth rates, inflation is money growth, plus the growth of velocity, minus the growth of output. It becomes a theory when velocity is stable and output grows for its own reasons, as in Act Five. Then, over long periods, inflation is simply money growth less output growth.

Here is the theory on the world's data. Each dot is a country: its average growth of broad money from 1990 to 2024, against its average inflation, on log scales. The correlation across 146 countries is 0.96. The slope is 0.96: a country whose money grew ten points faster had about ten points more inflation. Allowing for output growth, it is almost exactly one. Japan sits at the bottom left; Angola and Brazil are far up to the right. George McCandless and Warren Weber drew the same picture in 1995, for a hundred and ten countries over thirty years. Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz's monetary history of the United States, in 1963, had found it in a century of American data. In the long run, inflation is a monetary phenomenon.

But only in the long run. Take every year in every country where inflation was below ten percent, 3,550 country-years. The correlation between money growth and the same year's inflation is only 0.28. Over a year or two, velocity moves, output moves, and prices adjust slowly, so money and prices drift apart; Part thirty explains why prices are sticky. That is the series' fact: across countries and decades, inflation tracks money growth; over a year or two, it does not.

And velocity is not a constant of nature. Here is American M2's velocity: nominal GDP divided by the stock of broad money. In 1959, each dollar of M2 was spent about 1.8 times a year on output. It rose to about 2.2 by 1997, as interest rates and new financial products made holding money costlier. Then it fell, to about 1.4 now, with the low interest rates of the 2010s and the cash piles of the pandemic. Velocity moves with interest rates, innovation and fear: chapter nine asks why people hold money at all.
Hyper: Chapter six. Hyperinflation and the inflation tax.

Phillip Cagan defined a hyperinflation in 1956 as prices rising more than fifty percent a month. Steve Hanke and Nicholas Krus later listed every one they could document. Here are four peaks, on a log scale. Germany, October 1923: prices rose twenty-nine thousand five hundred percent in a month, doubling every few days. Yugoslavia, January 1994, and Zimbabwe, November 2008: prices doubled every day or so. And the record, Hungary in July 1946: forty-one quadrillion percent in a month, prices doubling about every fifteen hours.

Cagan's insight was about demand. People choose how much purchasing power to keep in money. He wrote the log of real balances as falling in proportion to expected inflation. When prices are expected to rise fast, people hold as little money as they can: workers are paid daily and spend their wages within hours. The constant, alpha, measured in months, was about five in Germany. And a government that prints money collects a tax: every holder of money loses purchasing power, and the government gains it. The tax rate is inflation; the tax base is real balances. Raise the rate, and the base shrinks.

Plot the revenue against the rate. At low inflation the tax raises little. As inflation rises, revenue rises, until people's flight from money outruns the higher rate. With alpha equal to five, revenue is highest at one over alpha: twenty percent a month. And even there it is only about 7.4 percent of the real balances people would hold at zero inflation, each month. Beyond the peak, printing faster raises less. A government that wants revenue should stop at twenty percent a month. None did.

Called it? The revenue theory says governments print money to pay their bills, and Cagan's estimates put the most they could raise at about twenty percent inflation a month. They went far beyond it. German prices rose three hundred and twenty-two percent a month on average from August 1922 to November 1923, and in most of Cagan's seven cases inflation ran above the rate that maximized revenue. Economists call it Cagan's paradox. The likeliest answers: expectations lag, so printing faster pays for a while before people catch up; and governments in collapse could not commit to stop. Wrong, as a forecast of what governments would do.
Ends: Chapter seven. How four big inflations ended.

In 1982 Thomas Sargent studied four of the hyperinflations that followed the First World War. Austria, Germany, Hungary and Poland had run large deficits, some burdened by reparations, and their central banks had financed them by printing. Austria stabilized in 1922, with a loan arranged by the League of Nations and a new central bank. Germany in November 1923, with a new currency and an end to central bank credit for the government. Hungary in 1924, again with a League loan and a balanced budget. And Poland in 1924, with tax reform. In each, prices stopped rising within weeks, at the moment the government credibly stopped paying its way with the printing press.

Sargent's reading was that these were changes of regime, not slow squeezes. People believed the new rules, because they were written into law and backed by outside lenders: budgets would balance, and the central bank could no longer lend to the state. So expected inflation collapsed at once, and with it the cost of holding money. People wanted their money balances back, so the quantity of money could keep growing for a while after the stabilization without pushing prices up: Cagan's demand, running in reverse. Critics, among them Elmus Wicker, have argued that the stabilizations were less painless than Sargent's account suggests. The lesson that survived is about credibility.

Agora shows why the fiscal regime is the key. Suppose a government runs a deficit worth 4 percent of the real balances people would hold at zero inflation, every month, and pays it by printing. Two inflation rates raise exactly that much: a low one, 5.6 percent a month, and a high one, 39 percent, on the far side of the Laffer peak. If people's expectations adapt slowly, the economy settles at the low one. If they adapt fast, as they do once people have lived through inflation, there is no stopping: inflation runs away. And a deficit larger than the most the inflation tax can ever raise has no steady state at all. Printing faster cannot close it; only closing the deficit can. That is what the four stabilizations did.
Modern: The twenty-first century has had its own. In Zimbabwe, from 2000, commercial farms were seized and redistributed, and farm output and exports fell sharply. The government ran deficits, and its central bank spent heavily on its own account, both paid for by printing. By November 2008, prices were rising about 80 billion percent a month, doubling about once a day. In January 2009 the central bank issued a note for one hundred trillion Zimbabwe dollars. Weeks later the country gave up its currency altogether and used American dollars and South African rand. Prices stopped rising almost at once.

Venezuela followed the same road a decade later. From 2014 the price of oil, almost all of its exports, collapsed, and output fell year after year. The government's deficits were financed by the central bank. In July 2018 the IMF projected inflation of one million percent for the year. That August the government struck five zeros off the currency, which changes the units but not the printing. What slowed it was the dollar: by the end of the decade many shops priced and took payment in dollars, and the bolívar's tax base had nearly vanished.

The framework of the last three chapters fits both. The cause: a deficit larger than taxes and loans could cover. The mechanism: printing, and then flight from money. The paradox: printing beyond the point where it raises any more. And the end: a fiscal regime people believe, or, when no one believes anything, someone else's money.
Demand: Chapter nine. The demand for money.

Why hold money at all, when bonds pay interest? Because you need it to pay for things. William Baumol and James Tobin turned that into arithmetic in the 1950s. You earn Y a month, keep it in bonds, and spend it evenly. Each trip to the bank to sell bonds for cash costs b. If you make n trips a month, you hold Y over two n in money on average. The cost is the interest you give up on that money plus the cost of the trips. Minimize it, and the best number of trips is the square root of i Y over two b. So money holdings rise with the square root of income and fall with the square root of the interest rate. Double your income and you hold only forty-one percent more money: there are economies of scale in managing cash.

On the Island, with an income of 3,000 coconuts a month and a cost of 2 per trip, here is money held against the interest rate. At one percent a month, an islander makes about 2.7 trips and holds about 550 on average. Raise the rate, and people economize: more trips, less money, and money turns over faster. That is why velocity rose with interest rates in chapter five.

Does the American data look like Baumol and Tobin? Plot money relative to income, as a log, against the interest rate, quarter by quarter. From 1959 to 1980, a tidy downward line: when rates rose, Americans held less money relative to income, about 6.7 percent less for each point. Then, in the 1980s, the relationship broke. Banks were allowed to offer accounts that paid interest and could be drawn on like money, and the line jumped. After 1994 a new line appears, flatter, at about 3.2 percent a point. By the late 1980s the Federal Reserve had stopped targeting M1 at all. Robert Lucas and Juan Pablo Nicolini argued in 2015 that adding the new money-market deposit accounts back in restores a stable demand. Money demand is stable only if you measure the right money.
Banks: Chapter ten. What money is today: banks and the central bank.

What is money today? Three things. Currency: notes and coins, which are the central bank's promise, and which anyone can hold. Reserves: the accounts banks keep at the central bank, its other kind of liability, which only banks can hold. And deposits: what your bank owes you. That is the money most people use. In the United States, currency is now only about 11 percent of M2. In Britain in 2013, the Bank of England counted ninety-seven percent of broad money as bank deposits. So the question is where deposits come from.

Watch two balance sheets. A bank with reserves, loans, deposits and capital, and Ana, who owns a bakery and wants to borrow a hundred to buy an oven. The bank approves the loan. It does not hand over anyone else's savings. It writes a new loan on the asset side, and a new deposit in Ana's name on the liability side, at the same moment. Ana now owns a deposit of a hundred and owes a hundred. Broad money has risen by a hundred, and the bank's reserves have not changed at all. When the loan is repaid, the deposit disappears again. In the words of the Bank of England's 2014 article, lending creates deposits.

That overturns a story still told in many textbooks. In the story, the central bank fixes reserves, banks lend out a multiple of them, and the money supply is a fixed multiple of base money. In 2007, M2 was about 9 times America's monetary base. Then, after the crisis, the Federal Reserve bought bonds on a vast scale and the base rose from about 837 billion dollars to about 4,075 billion. If the multiplier held, M2 should have multiplied too. It rose by about half. By 2014, M2 was only 2.8 times the base. Banks lend when lending pays, given the interest rate the central bank sets, and reserves follow. What the central bank controls is the price of reserves, not the quantity of money. Part thirty-one builds monetary policy on that.
Fisher: Chapter eleven. Money, interest and prices.

Money also shows up in interest rates. A lender who expects prices to rise five percent a year will want five points more interest, just to stay even. So the nominal interest rate is roughly the real rate plus expected inflation. Irving Fisher wrote this down in 1896. It means that in the long run, faster money growth brings higher interest rates, not lower ones. That is the opposite of the short run, when a central bank pushes rates down by supplying reserves, as Part thirty-one will show. The two are reconciled by time: the first effect is immediate, the second comes as expectations catch up.

In American data the two travel together. The three-month Treasury bill rate, and inflation over the previous twelve months, since 1960. Decade by decade, as inflation rose into the 1970s, so did interest rates, though in the 1970s not by enough: the real rate averaged -0.8 points, as lenders kept being surprised. In the 1980s, with inflation coming down, it averaged +3.3. The real rate moves, but much less than the nominal rate and inflation do. That is Fisher's point.

Two words for what money does not do. Neutrality: a once-and-for-all doubling of every amount of money, every price and every debt changes nothing real. It is a change of units, like Venezuela's lopped zeros. Superneutrality: a permanently faster rate of money growth changes nothing real either. Miguel Sidrauski showed in 1967 that in a growth model with money, the long-run capital stock does not depend on money growth. But inflation is a tax on holding money, and people spend time and effort avoiding it, so money growth is not quite neutral, as the next chapter measures. And in the short run, when prices are sticky, money moves output and jobs. That is the subject of Parts twenty-seven and thirty.
Optimum: Chapter twelve. The optimum quantity of money.

How much money should there be? Milton Friedman's answer, in 1969, starts from a gap. Printing money costs society almost nothing, but holding it costs each of us the interest we give up. So people make extra trips to the bank and keep balances too thin, economizing on something the economy could provide for free. Close the gap: make the nominal interest rate zero. By Fisher's equation that means inflation equal to minus the real rate. The Friedman rule: a gentle, steady deflation.

How much does the gap cost? Agora gives the Island cash in advance: islanders must buy today's consumption with money carried from yesterday. Inflation taxes that money, so they work and consume a little less. At the Friedman rule, a deflation of four percent a year here, the cost is zero. At ten percent inflation it is about 0.9 percent of consumption, every year, for ever. At fifty percent, about 8. Robert Lucas estimated in 2000, from a century of American money demand, that bringing inflation from ten percent to zero is worth slightly less than one percent of income. Small each year, large over a lifetime.

Yet no central bank follows the Friedman rule. When prices adjust slowly, a steady price level avoids other costs, which Part thirty measures. Interest rates kept near zero leave no room to cut them in a slump. And measured inflation slightly overstates the true rise in the cost of living, as Part three showed. So most central banks aim for about two percent a year, an inflation target, a practice New Zealand began in 1990. Part thirty-one asks why two.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dial: the interest semi-elasticity of money demand.

One dial, new in this part: the interest semi-elasticity of money demand, how much less money, relative to income, people hold for each point on the interest rate. Laurence Ball's estimate for American M1 after the Second World War was about -0.05: five percent less money per point. Peter Ireland, using the years after 1980 and Cagan's form, found it below two percent per point. This film's regressions, from chapter nine, give -0.067 before 1981 and -0.032 after 1994. The status: contested. The number decides how costly inflation is, and it depends on which accounts you call money.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: reserves and payments.

Chapter ten said the central bank sets the price of reserves. Here is how that works now. Before the crisis of 2008, American banks held about 44 billion dollars of reserves, kept scarce so that small changes moved the overnight rate. By 2014, after the Fed's bond purchases, about 2,842 billion. Since October 2008 the Fed has paid interest on reserves, and by setting that rate it sets a floor under what banks will lend for. In 2019 it said it would keep reserves ample for good. The New York Fed's trading desk now steers rates with administered rates and repurchase agreements, not by rationing the quantity of money.

Money's first job is paying. A payment between customers of different banks moves a deposit from one bank to the other, and the banks settle between themselves in reserves. Large payments go through systems like Fedwire, which settle each one at once in central bank money. Everyday payments, cards and transfers, are netted and settled in batches. In the last decade, instant payment systems have spread: India's UPI in 2016, Brazil's Pix in 2020, the Federal Reserve's FedNow in 2023. And in Kenya, M-Pesa, launched in 2007, turned the mobile phone into an account for millions who had none: Kocherlakota's memory, held by a phone company.

So: central bank desks steer rates and manage the balance sheet; bank treasurers manage liquidity and the cost of deposits; payment systems settle, guard against fraud and race to be instant; and finance ministries collect seigniorage and must resist the temptation of chapter six.
